blocks.text: What an AI assistant for designers on Mac actually does

An AI assistant for designers on Mac listens when you ask, looks at what is on your screen, and answers in plain language. It should point at the control you mean, explain why it behaves that way, and tell you the next step. It should not take over the app. That last part matters more than most people expect.

Lazur works this way. It lives in the notch at the top of your screen. You hold ⌥⌘ and ask about whatever is open. It answers out loud. Ask where something is, and it draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click before it moves on.

That split is the point. The assistant does the finding, the reading and the typing. You do the clicking, the design decisions and the sending. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it has no partnership with any app maker.
Where a designer's computer time actually goes

No study we found measures how designers spend their week. The numbers here cover knowledge workers in general. Use them as a starting point, then check your own week with a calendar and a simple tally.

Microsoft's 2023 Work Trend Index found that, within Microsoft 365, the average person spends 57% of their time communicating and 43% creating. That comes from Microsoft's own app activity. The page does not define what counts as creating, so read it as a rough signal, not a measurement of design work.

Asana's Anatomy of Work research, based on more than 10,000 knowledge workers, finds about a quarter of time goes to skills-based work. Another 13% goes to strategic planning. The remaining 60% goes to communicating about tasks, locating documents and handling shifting priorities. Asana names designing once as skills-based work, but gives no designer breakdown.

Two things stand out. Coordination takes more of the week than making things does, in both studies. Most of that coordination is searching, asking and switching. Those are the tasks an assistant can shorten without touching your design judgment.
The email and chat load behind those numbers

Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index surveyed 31,000 knowledge workers across 31 markets. The average worker receives 117 emails a day, and most are skimmed in under 60 seconds. A client thread can sit unread in a pile of internal chatter all morning.

The same report counts 153 Teams messages per weekday on average. It also finds an interruption every two minutes during core hours, 275 times a day, from meetings, email and chat. A two-minute interruption is short. Getting back into a dense Figma file after one is not.
Where the design apps fit into a Mac workday

Most designers on a Mac run several tools at once. Figma holds the layouts. An Adobe app handles photos or icons. Canva makes social cuts. Slack and Linear carry the decisions. Each one has its own menus and shortcuts, and an assistant earns its place when it can work across all of them.

Figma's desktop app for Mac needs macOS 12 or later, according to Figma's help guide. Figma also says support for older versions is removed six months after a release. The minimum can change, so check the live requirements before you upgrade or buy a new machine.

Open file tabs sit in the navigation bar in the desktop app. The tab menu in the top right lists open and recently closed tabs across all windows. If you present often, go to View > Always Show Tabs When Presenting. That option is available only on Mac.
Adobe costs: check which plan you need before you buy

Adobe lists Photoshop and Illustrator as single apps at US$22.99 a month each, on an annual plan billed monthly. Creative Cloud Standard is US$54.99 a month. The Photography plan is US$19.99 a month. These are US prices from Adobe's plans page, and they can change.

blocks.text: Adobe's Creative Cloud Pro is listed at US$34.99 a month for the first three months for new subscribers, then US$69.99 a month. That intro rate is the number to watch. Put the end date in Apple Reminders the day you sign up. Lazur can set that reminder by voice.
Where a voice assistant helps inside each app
In Figma, Lazur helps with settings you cannot find, such as Auto layout, component properties and export. It points at the panel and explains the option. It does not change the setting for you.

In Photoshop, the command you need is often one menu deeper than you expect. Image > Image Size is the usual route for a client who wants a bigger file. The shortcut is ⌥⌘I. Ask Lazur to point at the menu, then press the shortcut yourself.
In Canva, Lazur explains resize and brand kit options in plain words. It can draft captions when you dictate the brief. You still check every caption against the brand rules before you post.

In Slack and Linear, Lazur reads the open window and tells you which threads or tickets need a decision today. It drafts replies on request. Hold fn when you want to speak a reply instead of typing it.
A worked example: dictating a handoff note

Say you finish a card component late in the afternoon. The handoff note should cover the states, the spacing values, what breaks on small screens, the copy still pending and the file link. Speaking a note like that is often faster than typing it. You can test that with the speaking vs typing test below.

Put the cursor in the Slack message to the developer, hold fn, and speak the note. Read it back before you send it. Dictation trips on product names, component names and file names, so check those first. Fix them once, then add them to your personal dictionary so they stick.

Store the standard closing line as a snippet. Say the short phrase, and the full line appears at the cursor. Clipboard slots keep the file link handy for the next note. The same text can then go into a Linear ticket without retyping anything.
To test the speed gap first, try the [speaking vs typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test). For the Slack setup, see [AI assistant for Slack on Mac](/apps/slack).
Mistakes designers make with an AI assistant

items: Asking it for a design verdict. Ask what a setting does, not whether the layout is good. A taste call belongs to you and your client.
Trusting dictated names. Speech tools mishear product and file names. Read every name before it goes into a file, a ticket or an email.
Expecting it to click. Lazur points and guides. You do the click, and Lazur waits for it.
Forgetting the hold. Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut. Release the key and it stops.
Sharing unreleased client work without checking the rules. Your contract and your employer decide what can leave your machine.
Skipping the test run. Try one real task in your own file during the first session, then check the answer in the app.

blocks.text: Privacy, client work and the rules you still follow
Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models.

That is the vendor's policy. It does not decide what your client allows. Many studios and agencies have written rules on unreleased work, NDAs and third-party tools. Read those rules before you hold the key over a client file. If the rules are unclear, ask your account lead or legal contact.

blocks.title: Check the contract first
blocks.text: If an NDA or client contract covers unreleased designs, do not show those files to any AI tool until your employer or client says it is allowed. Lazur's privacy policy does not replace their rules.
Price, platform and where to start on Mac

Lazur is a Mac app for Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. It starts with a trial, and no credit card is needed. The current plans are on the [pricing page](/pricing). Check that page for exact amounts, since it is the source to trust for them.
Download Lazur from the [download page](/download). Grant the permissions it asks for, then test both keys. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask about the open app. Then hold fn and dictate one line into a text field.
A first-week checklist for designers

items: Open Lazur once after you install it, and check that it appears in the notch.
Hold ⌥⌘ and ask what the open panel does. Listen for the spoken answer.
Ask where one control is. Watch for the circle and the label.
Hold fn and dictate a single line into a Slack draft. Read it back before you send.
Ask Lazur to walk you through one task you repeat every week, one click at a time.

blocks.text: The job market and why your time matters

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics counted about 253,100 graphic designer jobs in 2025, with median pay of $62,960 a year. It projects a 2% employment decline from 2025 to 2035, a net change of about 4,200 jobs. The drop is small, but it means fewer openings to go around.

Use the job numbers to set goals, not to panic. A tool that saves a few minutes a day only matters if you spend that time on design work. Measure where the minutes go before you decide what to automate.
Who should skip this

Skip it if your studio blocks AI tools, and wait until someone checks the rules. Skip it if you mostly sketch on paper, since a voice assistant adds little there. Skip it if you want a tool that clicks for you. Lazur is built to point and guide, not to operate the app.
What to do next

Pick one app and one slow task. Track how often you ask for help and where you get stuck. Use that log to decide whether the subscription fits your work. Your own week tells you more than any feature list.

faq.question: Is Lazur an AI assistant for designers on Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Lazur is a voice assistant for macOS that sees your screen only while you hold the shortcut. It answers out loud and points at controls. It runs on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.

faq.question: Does Lazur work inside Figma and Photoshop?
faq.answer: It works alongside them, in any app. It sees the open window, points at controls and explains settings. It is not a plugin or add-in for Figma or Adobe, and it has no partnership with either company.

faq.question: Will Lazur click buttons or edit my files?
faq.answer: No. Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. It does not operate other apps for you. You make every change in the app yourself.

faq.question: What does the Figma desktop app need on a Mac?
faq.answer: Figma's help guide says the desktop app needs macOS 12 or later. Figma removes support for older versions six months after a release, so check the live requirements before you upgrade.

faq.question: Is my client work sent to AI providers?
faq.answer: Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, only while you hold the shortcut. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Your contract still decides what you may share.

faq.question: How much do Adobe apps cost on a Mac?
faq.answer: On Adobe's US plans page, the Photoshop and Illustrator single apps are US$22.99 a month each on an annual plan billed monthly. Creative Cloud Standard is US$54.99 a month. Prices change, so check the page before you buy.

faq.question: How do I dictate into Figma comments or Slack?
faq.answer: Place the cursor in the text field, hold fn, and speak. Dictation writes clean text at the cursor in any app. Read it back before you send, especially names and file links.

faq.question: Can I try Lazur before I pay?
faq.answer: Yes. It starts with a trial, and no credit card is needed. The trial starts when you first open the app. Check the pricing page for current plan details.

demo.spoken: Why won't this card stay the same height when the title wraps?
demo.context: Figma desktop on a Mac, a product card frame with a title that wraps to two lines
demo.result: Lazur circles the Auto layout section in the right panel and explains the fixed height setting.
demo.output: Your card has a fixed height, so the wrapped title pushes text past the bottom edge. Select the card frame and look at the Auto layout section on the right. Set the height to Hug contents, so the card grows with its text. If the frame is not an Auto layout frame yet, press ⇧A to add one. Then set the title to Fill container for the width.
